channel.title: Zach Koncir: writing
channel.description: Zach Koncir builds open source tools that keep engineers in charge of their AI agents, and helps teams learn to use them well.

item.title: Pave the road
item.description: It took me months to get AI agents working for me. My team shouldn't have to pay that cost again, one engineer at a time.
item.content:encoded:
In The day it clicked, I wrote about the months it took before AI agents started working for me. The models were never the hard part. Changing how I work was. So was getting the agent access to every tool I use, and building a harness I’d trust at work.

I got through it mostly on my own. Then I looked around.

A lot of the engineers on my team were stuck in exactly the same place. Same questions, same missing access, same uneasy feeling about letting an agent loose on real systems. Every one of them was about to pay the cost I had just paid, separately, one engineer at a time.

That’s the part I couldn’t let go of.

Why it falls to tech leads

I don’t think every engineer should have to become a tooling expert before an agent is useful to them. Most of them are heads down on delivery. They don’t have a few spare weeks to wire up integrations and figure out guardrails, and they shouldn’t need them.

Tech leads are in a different spot. We already touch a lot of systems, a little at a time, so we’ve usually done most of the wiring once already. We also see the whole team. When five people hit the same wall in the same week, that isn’t five problems. It’s one problem that keeps getting paid for.

So the job is simple to describe: pay the setup cost once, so your team doesn’t pay it over and over.

What I’m paving

I’m building a shared set of tools for my team. Nothing exotic, just the things I wish I’d had on day one.

  • Connectors. Access to the systems people use every day, so the agent can actually see what they see. The token helper and observability connector from the last post are good examples. Building them took me real time. Using them should take nobody any.
  • Guardrails. Checks that stop the agent from doing things it shouldn’t. This is the part that makes people comfortable trying it on real work, and the part almost nobody builds for themselves.
  • Shared setup. A common config and set of skills everyone can start from, instead of a blank page.
  • Docs and onboarding. A way in that doesn’t need me in the room.

What I’m deliberately not sharing: prompts

The first thing most teams build is a shared prompt library. I’m not building one, on purpose.

A copied prompt means someone else did the thinking. The whole point is that the engineer stays in charge. You own what ships, no matter who typed it, and that’s hard to do when you’re running someone else’s instructions.

If you don’t understand a prompt, you can’t tell when its output is wrong. A prompt you wrote yourself comes with a sense of what good looks like. A borrowed one doesn’t.

Everyone works differently. The agent should adapt to the engineer, not the other way round. A prompt that fits how I think might be exactly wrong for how you do.

Prompts don’t travel well. On a team where people use different harnesses and different models, the same prompt can behave very differently from one setup to the next. It looks shared, but it isn’t really the same thing for everyone.

So the rule I’m working with is: share the road, not the driving. Tools, access and guardrails are shared. How you talk to the agent, and what you decide, stays yours.

The response so far

I’ve shown it to a bunch of engineers, and to people who aren’t engineers at all. The reaction has been the same: when can I have it?

The non-engineers surprised me most. I’d been thinking of this as an engineering problem. It turns out the wall I hit, too much setup before anything useful happens, is in front of a lot more people than I expected.

If you’re a tech lead

You probably went through some version of my months already. That experience is worth more than it feels like. You know where the walls are, because you hit them.

Look at your team and find the wall they keep hitting. Then take it down once, for everyone.

item.title: The day it clicked
item.description: I struggled with AI agents for months. Then I answered a hard question about a system I'd never touched, in about an hour, while juggling other projects.
item.content:encoded:
For months, I didn’t get it.

The models weren’t the hard part. Everything around them was. I had to figure out how to change the way I work, get the agent access to all the tools I use, and build a harness that fit. As a tech lead, my day doesn’t look like a typical engineer’s on a team. I touch a lot of systems, a little at a time, and every one of them needed wiring up.

I bounced between tools. One got ruled out for policy reasons. Another never quite fit. Then I landed on pi, and it just worked. It was minimal and fast, and I could bend it to how I work. It also had almost no guardrails. The model could drive tools pretty much however it wanted, and that’s not something I could take to work and feel good about.

So I finally set aside real time to figure it out: the integrations, the habits, and the guardrails I wished it had. Somewhere along the way, without a single big moment, it changed. I stopped asking the agent to do my job and started asking it to carry the parts of the job that wear me down. Then a ticket landed that showed me how far that had gone.

The question

A couple of months earlier, a web application firewall in front of one of our busiest APIs had started blocking real users. It was running a strict OWASP ruleset, and normal traffic had crept close enough to the blocking threshold that it tipped over. By the time anyone declared an incident, it had been going for hours.

The follow-up ticket asked a simple question: how much headroom do we have now, and can we monitor it so this doesn’t happen again?

I knew what a WAF was. I knew how anomaly scoring works and roughly where I’d look. What I didn’t know was this vendor. I’d never logged into it, never read its docs, never used its analytics API. Normally that’s a day or two of reading before you even start on the actual question. Tasks like this sit in a backlog for a week while everyone hopes someone else picks them up.

About an hour

I gave the agent the ticket, the incident write-up and the question. Then I mostly went back to what I was building that day, and checked in between other work.

The first thing it needed was access. It didn’t have the integrations, so we built them on the spot: a small helper for storing and loading API tokens, and a connector to our observability platform. It could read the firewall config, but the audit trail didn’t go back far enough to show who had changed what, and when. It said so plainly instead of guessing at the history.

Then it got to work, and it came back with things I didn’t expect.

  • The question couldn’t be answered as asked. The firewall only logs the anomaly score when a request gets blocked. Near-misses aren’t recorded anywhere, so true headroom can’t be measured today. That’s not a guess. It’s a finding, and it changed the whole ticket.
  • One outlier. It audited every zone we have. One was running a far stricter ruleset than the rest, and it was seeing about fifty times more challenges than the next busiest.
  • A backtest. It replayed two months of data against a simple rule: alert when blocks run 1.3 times higher than the same hour four weeks running. That rule would have fired before the original incident started, hours before anyone declared it.

It proposed three ways to monitor this going forward. I picked one. When it reported the numbers, I asked how much to trust them, since the analytics are sampled. It checked: totals were stable on busy paths, noisy on quiet ones, so the alert needs a volume floor.

Counting the time to set up the tooling, I spent about an hour on it. Spread across an evening, flipping between this and two other projects.

Three months earlier, I’d have blocked off a day or two, and I’d have come back with a less useful answer.

I’m not going to pretend I stayed calm about it. For a while afterward I felt like Bradley Cooper in Limitless: the same brain, suddenly with access to everything it had ever half-read. The difference is that my pill came with an audit trail.

What actually changed

The agent didn’t know anything I couldn’t have looked up. That’s the point. What it removed was the cost of looking it up. The understanding was still mine: what a WAF is for, what a good alert looks like, which of three options was worth recommending, and when a number needed a second look. The vendor trivia was the part I’d never need again.

That’s the shift I keep coming back to. Work that took a day or two now takes under an hour, not because the work got easier but because the slow parts did. And context switching, which used to be the most expensive thing an engineer did, is getting close to free. I proved that to myself by doing it three times in one evening.

It only worked because I was in the loop. The agent made assumptions, like every model does. I made the decisions. I wrote more about that in Engineers in charge, which is the closest thing I have to a summary of everything I learned the slow way.

If you’re still in the months where it doesn’t click, I’ve been there. Pick one boring task you hate and make the agent carry it. Start there.
